title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: The Forensic Ledger — Ten Years of Profit, Cash & Balance Sheet Quality

epigraph.quote: Over a single year, working capital is timing; over a decade, working capital is destiny.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Rule

web_blocks.html: A ten-year sweep of Marine Electricals' consolidated accounts (FY15–FY26, plus H1 FY27/TTM) shows strong growth paired with cash-conversion friction [1]. Revenue compounded at 12.7% a year from ₹236 crore in FY15 to ₹877 crore in FY26, reaching ₹1,152 crore TTM [1]. Net Profit grew from ₹9 crore to ₹59 crore (35.5% 5-year PAT CAGR) and ₹80 crore TTM [1].

web_blocks.caption: 10-Year Consolidated Profit & Loss Summary (FY17–FY26 & TTM)
web_blocks.takeaway: Sales expanded 3.2x from FY17 (₹272 Cr) to FY26 (₹877 Cr), with OPM breaking out of its historical 8–9% range to 11% in FY26 and TTM [1].

web_blocks.html: Summing the Cash Flow statement over ten years (FY17–FY26) reveals the core forensic warning [1]. Cumulative Net Profit totaled ₹209 crore, while cumulative Cash from Operating Activities (CFO) totaled just ₹93 crore [1]. That equals a 10-year CFO/PAT conversion ratio of only 44.5% [1]. After capex and acquisitions, cumulative Free Cash Flow over FY17–FY26 was negative ₹48 crore [1].

web_blocks.caption: 10-Year Consolidated Cash Flow & Free Cash Flow Forensics (FY17–FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: In 5 of the last 10 years (FY19, FY21, FY23, FY24, FY26), Free Cash Flow was negative; cumulative 10Y FCF is -₹48 Cr despite ₹209 Cr of cumulative PAT [1].

web_blocks.html: The Balance Sheet shows how the firm bridged that cash gap without distress [1]. Total Borrowings rose from ₹37 crore in FY22 to ₹97 crore in FY24, dropped to ₹55 crore in FY25 after the ₹108.22 crore equity raise, and stood at ₹94 crore in September 2026 [1, 8]. Against ₹539 crore of equity, Debt/Equity is a modest ~0.17x [1, 8]. Meanwhile, 'Other Assets' (mainly receivables and contract assets) swelled from ₹319 crore in FY22 to ₹775 crore in FY26 and ₹953 crore in September 2026 [1]. That bucket now makes up 87% of total assets (₹1,096 crore) [1]. Year-by-year CFO-to-EBITDA swings highlight that working-capital sensitivity [1]. Conversion hit 118% in FY18, dropped to -205% in FY19, reached 167% in FY22, fell to 4% in FY24, and swung from 106% in FY25 to 6% in FY26 [1]. Fixed Assets plus CWIP stood at just ₹138 crore (12.6% of total assets) in September 2026 [1]. With 87% of assets tied up in Other Assets, cash collection remains the decisive balance-sheet test [1].

Footnote, Litigation & Consolidated Audit Forensics: Reading beyond the headline balance sheet reveals material contingent exposures and recurring consolidated audit exceptions [4, 5]. First, an August 1, 2024 final arbitration award on a legacy 50 MW solar EPC dispute directed payment of ₹21.34 crore plus interest to sub-contractor GE Power Conversion Limited (totaling a ₹31.36 crore payout exposure). Second, the FY26 Annual Report discloses an unresolved ₹14.88 crore GST demand (dated October 23, 2024, currently under appeal) alongside an ~₹16 crore IBC refund claim plus interest against State Bank of India pending before the NCLT as of March 31, 2026. Third, while standalone audit opinions remained unmodified from FY21 through FY26, consolidated audits carry recurring exceptions: a going-concern Emphasis of Matter at subsidiary Eltech Engineers Madras Pvt. Ltd., accounting software audit-trail exceptions (database-level, inventory-module, and Excel payroll gaps), and ~₹8 crore of consolidated goodwill from loss-making Canadian subsidiary Xanatos Marine Ltd. carried without impairment through FY26.

web_blocks.caption: 10-Year Consolidated Balance Sheet Structure (FY17–Sep 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Net worth expanded from ₹75 Cr (FY17) to ₹539 Cr (Sep 2026) via retained earnings and equity raises, keeping debt low (0.17x D/E) even as Other Assets hit ₹953 Cr [1].

web_blocks.caption: Working Capital & Return Ratios (FY17–FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: ROCE recovered from 9% (FY20) to 18% (FY26), while 3-year average ROE remains muted at 12.1% (13.1% latest) due to the enlarged equity base and 178 debtor days [1].

web_blocks.mechanism: Tecpro Systems booked rapid revenue growth on long-gestation Balance-of-Plant and industrial contracts where milestone billing, retention money, and client disputes caused receivables to compound faster than collections, eventually triggering a bank-guarantee and liquidity freeze.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Debtor days spiraled past 2,500–2,900 days and working capital stretched beyond 3,400 days against ₹4,000+ Cr of liabilities; admitted to NCLT CIRP in August 2017 and ordered into liquidation in January 2020 [18, 19]. (Peer Jyoti Structures similarly saw 1,000+ debtor days and NFB limit freezes in 2017 [20].)
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Marine Electricals' 0.17x Debt/Equity and ICRA A- rating place it worlds away from Tecpro's debt load, and its 6–12 month data-center cycle is far shorter than power-plant EPC. Nevertheless, Tecpro is the canonical Indian base rate proving that rising profits paired with uncollected receivables can turn fatal if bank-guarantee rollovers ever tighten.

web_blocks.title: Forensic Audit Summary: Bull vs. Bear on Cash & Governance
paragraphs: Bull Case: Low debt (₹94 Cr gross debt vs ₹539 Cr equity), an [ICRA]A- rating, 50-day inventory turns, and 18% ROCE show a sound balance sheet backing ₹3,514 Cr in orders [1, 4, 7].

Bear Case: 10-year CFO/PAT of 44.5%, negative ₹48 Cr cumulative FCF, ₹953 Cr in Other Assets (178 debtor days), unresolved ₹31.36 Cr arbitration and ₹14.88 Cr GST contingencies, consolidated audit exceptions (Eltech going concern, audit-trail gaps, unimpaired Xanatos goodwill), 12.1% 3-year ROE, and a 7.68-point promoter stake drop since Dec 2023 demand strict cash-collection and governance proof [1, 5].

book_paragraphs: Numbers on a profit-and-loss statement are an opinion; ten years of cumulative cash flows are a verdict. When we lay out Marine Electricals' financial history from FY15 through September 2026, two very different stories emerge side by side.

On the income statement, the growth is undeniable. Revenue climbed from 236 crore rupees in FY15 to 877 crore rupees in FY26, and hit 1,152 crore rupees on a trailing twelve-month basis. Net profit grew at a 35.5 percent five-year compound rate, reaching 59 crore rupees in FY26 and 80 crore rupees trailing. Operating margins have stepped up to 11 percent, and return on capital employed has recovered from 9 percent in the pandemic trough to 18 percent.

Now flip to the cash flow statement and add up the entire ten years from FY17 through FY26. Across that decade, Marine Electricals reported 209 crore rupees of cumulative net profit. How much operating cash did it generate over those same ten years? Just 93 crore rupees—barely 44.5 percent of reported earnings. After subtracting capital expenditures and bolt-on investments, cumulative free cash flow over ten years was negative 48 crore rupees.

Look at the balance sheet and footnotes to see where every rupee went—and what liabilities sit off the headline ledger. Total assets stood at 1,096 crore rupees in September 2026, and 953 crore rupees of that—87 percent of the entire balance sheet—sat in 'Other Assets', dominated by trade receivables and contract work-in-progress. To keep the engine running without overloading on debt, the company raised equity in 2018 and 2024, keeping borrowings modest at 94 crore rupees against 539 crore rupees of net worth (0.17x debt-to-equity). Yet footnote forensics reveal three unresolved overhangs: a 31.36 crore rupee arbitration payout exposure from a legacy 50 MW solar EPC dispute with GE Power Conversion (21.34 crore rupees principal plus interest), a 14.88 crore rupee disputed GST demand under appeal, and an approximate 16 crore rupee IBC refund claim against State Bank of India pending before the NCLT. Furthermore, while standalone audits were clean from FY21 through FY26, consolidated audits carry recurring exceptions—including a going-concern Emphasis of Matter at subsidiary Eltech Engineers Madras, accounting software audit-trail gaps, and 8 crore rupees of unimpaired goodwill on loss-making Canadian unit Xanatos Marine.

Still, history offers a sobering base rate for Indian project contractors that let receivables outrun cash. Consider Tecpro Systems between 2011 and 2017: rapid top-line growth masked severe milestone and retention-money lockups until debtor days exploded past 2,500 days, banks froze non-fund-based guarantees, and the company entered NCLT insolvency in 2017 and liquidation in 2020. Marine Electricals is nowhere near Tecpro's debt load or duration risk—its data-center cycle turns in months, not years—but the lesson is timeless: in project engineering, you must watch Debtor Days, CFO/PAT, and contingent-liability footnotes like a hawk.

book_callouts.title: The Quality Verdict
book_callouts.text: Marine Electricals is a genuine growth business with real engineering credentials, but its 44.5 percent ten-year CFO-to-PAT conversion and 178-day receivables keep it firmly in the cyclical-conditional camp until cash collection catches up with the order book.

book_subsections.title: Ten Years of Numbers: Separating Accounting Growth from Cash
paragraphs: Let's sit down with the full ten-year financial ledger from FY17 through FY26 and ask the hardest forensic question in investing: is Marine Electricals a genuine cash-compounding machine, or a working-capital-intensive project business? Over the decade, revenue expanded nearly 3.2x from ₹272 Cr (FY17) to ₹877 Cr (FY26), and net profit grew from ₹13 Cr to ₹59 Cr — a respectable 35.5% five-year profit CAGR on Screener.in.

Now look at the cash-flow statement across those exact same ten years. Operating cash flow was positive in six years and negative in four (FY19: -₹53 Cr, FY23: -₹2 Cr, FY24: -₹7 Cr, FY26: -₹16 Cr). Sum all ten years together: ₹209 Cr of cumulative PAT produced just ₹93 Cr of cumulative CFO (44.5% conversion) and -₹48 Cr of cumulative free cash flow. Meanwhile, Other Assets ballooned from ₹171 Cr in FY17 to ₹775 Cr in FY26 and ₹953 Cr by September 2026 — representing 87% of the entire ₹1,096 Cr balance sheet.

That is why our historical failure base-rate twin, Tecpro Systems, is such an important cautionary study. Tecpro also rode an infrastructure order-book boom with rising accounting profits while debtor days quietly climbed past 200 days and cash conversion collapsed, eventually ending in insolvency when credit lines tightened. Marine Electricals is in far better shape today — carrying low net debt (D/E 0.17x) and an upgraded [ICRA]A- rating — which is why we grade it CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL rather than a fail. Still, the cash-conversion gap disqualifies it from compounder status until proven otherwise.

book_subsections.title: Balance Sheet Stress-Test: Debt, Contingent Liabilities & Asset Quality
paragraphs: Let's run a quick forensic stress test on the September 2026 balance sheet. Total liabilities and equity stood at ₹1,096 Cr, backed by ₹539 Cr of net worth (₹28 Cr equity capital plus ₹511 Cr reserves), ₹94 Cr of borrowings, and ₹463 Cr of Other Liabilities (primarily trade payables and customer advances). On the surface, a 0.17x debt-to-equity ratio looks conservative and clean.

Look closer at the asset side, however: Fixed Assets plus CWIP total just ₹138 Cr (12.6% of total assets), while Other Assets — receivables, inventories, contract assets, and advances — stand at ₹953 Cr (87.0% of total assets). That asset-composition ratio tells you everything about the business model's risk profile. Marine Electricals is not a heavy-machinery manufacturer with hard plant collateral; it is a working-capital balance sheet. If even 10% of that ₹953 Cr in Other Assets is delayed or disputed during a data-center or shipyard slowdown, the ₹94 Cr debt load and ₹17 Cr–₹19 Cr annual interest bill suddenly loom much larger against negative free cash flow.

book_subsections.title: Working Capital Days & The CFO/EBITDA Volatility Pattern
paragraphs: Look closely at the year-by-year CFO-to-EBITDA conversion table in Screener.in from FY17 through FY26: 74% (FY17), 118% (FY18), -205% (FY19), 111% (FY20), 18% (FY21), 167% (FY22), 13% (FY23), 4% (FY24), 106% (FY25), and 6% (FY26). Notice that pattern: every time revenue surges rapidly — +36% in FY18 followed by FY19's cash crunch, +40% in FY24, and the FY26–H1 FY27 backlog ramp — operating cash flow collapses the very next year as receivables absorb all the profit.

True compounders convert 80%+ of EBITDA into operating cash flow year after year regardless of growth rate. A business whose CFO/EBITDA swings from 106% to 6% in a single year is telling you unambiguously that its growth is working-capital financed.
